body:
Hmm. I'm not a big fan of this approach, but willing to be convinced. To me, the cons are:
- Less explicit. script elements carry a lot of state unrelated to fetching scripts; by reading the algorithm, you can no longer tell what the relevant inputs are.
- Doesn't always apply, as in the worker case. Here you handle that by making the script optional.
- Seems like it would be awkward if we ever added these features to workers (`new Worker("url.js", { nonce: ... })`). In that case the current setup is better, where the caller disentangles the specific representation of the inputs (DOM attributes, dictionary members, ...) from their role in the fetching process.

I noticed that the spec currently says

> To fetch a classic script for a script element _element_

But the _element_ variable is unused; IMO we should remove it, instead of expanding its role.

The conversation in https://github.com/w3c/webappsec-csp/issues/70 provides some context for the suggestion.

> Less explicit.

I agree that the current setup is more explicit, but I'm not convinced that that's a good thing, as the explicitness just requires us to pass multiple arguments into various algorithms. For the same reason that it's nice to move to dictionaries, structs, and classes in "real" code, it seems nice to move to a higher-level structure in pseudo-code.

> Doesn't always apply, as in the worker case. Here you handle that by making the script optional.

Yes, it's an optional argument. That seems normal enough?

> Seems like it would be awkward if we ever added these features to workers.

I agree with this, but since we already separate out "[fetch a classic script](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#fetch-a-classic-script)" and "[fetch a classic worker script](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#fetch-a-classic-worker-script)", I'm not convinced that it's fatal. Are you planning on merging those algorithms at some point?

> I agree that the current setup is more explicit, but I'm not convinced that that's a good thing, as the explicitness just requires us to pass multiple arguments into various algorithms. For the same reason that it's nice to move to dictionaries, structs, and classes in "real" code, it seems nice to move to a higher-level structure in pseudo-code.

Sure, and if we had a dictionary, that would be fine. But you're passing the whole script element, which comes along with a lot of unnecessary state, so you can no longer tell what the inputs are to the algorithm. If you wanted to describe a "script fetch metadata" struct of some sort, that'd be OK I guess...

> Yes, it's an optional argument. That seems normal enough?

In this case, it effectively causes branching into two algorithms.

> I agree with this, but since we already separate out "fetch a classic script" and "fetch a classic worker script", I'm not convinced that it's fatal. Are you planning on merging those algorithms at some point?

That's more historical than anything else. For module script trees we don't.

Ok. It's not clear to me why a "script fetch metadata" is any clearer at the callsite than passing in the element itself, and seems like it would turn into an even bigger patch than this one. _shrug_ Your call. :)

I'll close this out, and send y'all a patch that just adds another argument instead to address w3c/webappsec-csp#70, and we can revisit if/when there's more of an issue with parameter overload than there is today.

> Ok. It's not clear to me why a "script fetch metadata" is any clearer at the callsite than passing in the element itself, and seems like it would turn into an even bigger patch than this one.

Just to maybe help clarify: the element contains a ton of state. All of its attributes' values, which can change over time; the already started/parser-inserted/non-blocking/ready to be parser-executed/from an external file flags, the script's type, and the script's script (a concept-script).

The current fetching algorithms are designed to take as input a number of known values, and return a concept-script. They're completely separate from DOM elements, and are in some sense "pure" in that they don't mutate any of their arguments.

In contrast, the "prepare a script" algorithm details how to take a `script` element, extract some relevant information from its attributes, flags, and from ambient state, pass those in to the more pure fetching algorithm to get back a concept-script, and then mutate various properties of the `script` element (including setting its concept-script to the return value of fetching).

I like this separation between impure, mutates-everything, needs-everything "prepare a script", and the more pure, inputs -> concept-script "fetch a script" algorithms.

What you're proposing would either move us toward a world where these get mushed together, or at least give the appearance of doing so. If fetching takes a `script` element, it seems quite possible to the reader it's going to consult any of those many many pieces of internal state, and possibly start mutating them too.

>  If fetching takes a script element, it seems quite possible to the reader it's going to consult any of those many many pieces of internal state, and possibly start mutating them too.

FWIW, this is in fact how it works in Chromium. We ship the element around to the point at which we create our internal analog to Fetch's "request", and read various bits of data off of it (see `ScriptLoader::fetchScript`). So far, nothing has exploded. :)
